summary: Provides an architectural overview of Remote ATtestation procedureS (RATS). It describes the entities that generate, convey, and evaluate evidentiary claims so one end can learn whether the other is in an intended operating state. The model is neutral toward processor architectures and claim contents. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Before sharing a secret, you want proof the other computer is not tampered with. This describes the roles in that check: someone shows evidence and someone judges it.

subtitle: The shared vocabulary and data flows for letting one machine prove to another that it is in a trustworthy state.

tldr.problem: A system that wants to deal with another system needs a way to know whether that other system is in a good state, and existing attestation solutions use different words for the same ideas.
tldr.mechanism: An Attester produces Evidence about itself, a Verifier appraises it against policy and reference values, and a Relying Party uses the resulting Attestation Results to decide what to allow. Two patterns, the Passport Model and the Background-Check Model, show how the messages can flow.
tldr.outcome: It defines a common set of roles, artifacts and freshness options for solution designers. No wire protocol is defined here.

facts.label: Supporting roles
facts.value: Endorser, Reference Value Provider, Verifier Owner, Relying Party Owner

today: RFC 9334 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines an architecture and vocabulary only; the data formats and wire protocols are left to other specifications.

sections.title: Why Remote Attestation Needs an Architecture
sections.content:
Systems that have been attested and verified to be in a good state can improve overall system posture, while systems that cannot be can be given reduced access or privileges, taken out of service, or flagged for repair. The RFC gives examples such as a bank backend that refuses to transact with a system not known to be in a good state.

In Remote ATtestation procedureS (RATS), one peer (the Attester) produces believable information about itself (Evidence) so a remote peer (the Relying Party) can decide whether to treat it as trustworthy. A third party, the Verifier, appraises the Evidence and creates Attestation Results. The document defines a universal set of terms so different solutions can be mapped onto one canonical architecture.

It also separates two ideas: trust is a choice one makes about another system, and trustworthiness is a quality of that system that informs the choice. Its reference use cases include network endpoint assessment, confidential machine learning model and data protection, critical infrastructure control, Trusted Execution Environment provisioning, a hardware watchdog, and FIDO biometric authentication.
sections.eli5: It is like a club that only lets in kids who can show they are wearing the right uniform. Someone shows the uniform, someone checks it, and the doorkeeper decides.

sections.title: Roles, Artifacts and Environments
sections.content:
The Attester creates Evidence. The Verifier applies an Appraisal Policy for Evidence, using the Evidence plus any Reference Values and Endorsements, and generates Attestation Results. The Relying Party applies its own Appraisal Policy for Attestation Results to make an application decision, such as authorization.

Supporting roles supply the inputs. An Endorser, typically a manufacturer, produces Endorsements that vouch for an Attester's capabilities. A Reference Value Provider produces Reference Values to compare Claims against. The Verifier Owner and Relying Party Owner, typically administrators, configure the two appraisal policies. An entity can take on several roles at once, and several entities can cooperate to implement one role.

Inside an Attester, an Attesting Environment collects Claims from a Target Environment and signs them as Evidence. In layered attestation, each stage measures the next, for example a ROM measures the bootloader and the bootloader then measures the kernel. A composite device is made of several sub-entities, each an Attester, with one lead Attester conveying combined Evidence to the Verifier.
sections.eli5: One kid shows a report card, a teacher checks it against the school rules, and a parent decides whether to allow a sleepover. The report card printer and the rule writers help behind the scenes.

sections.title: Passport and Background-Check Models
sections.content:
In the Passport Model, the Attester sends Evidence to the Verifier and gets back an Attestation Result that it treats as opaque. It can cache the result and present it to one or more Relying Parties, like a passport shown at an immigration desk. Since the Attestation Result travels in the resource access protocol, interoperability and standardization matter more for Attestation Results than for Evidence.

In the Background-Check Model, the Attester sends Evidence to the Relying Party, which treats it as opaque and forwards it to a Verifier, then compares the returned Attestation Result with its own policy. Any serialization format can be used for the Evidence, since the Relying Party does not parse it.

The choice depends on the use case, and one device may use both models at once. The Relying Party and Verifier may also be on the same machine, in which case no protocol is needed between them. The Passport Model can fail in three ways: the Verifier does not issue a positive result, the Relying Party's policy is not satisfied, or the Verifier is unreachable.
sections.eli5: With a passport, you get your stamped paper first and then show it at the door. With a background check, the doorkeeper phones the office to check you out. Both end with the doorkeeper deciding.

sections.title: Trust, Conceptual Messages and Freshness
sections.content:
Trust is expressed by storing trust anchors (a certificate, a raw public key or a symmetric key) in a trust anchor store. A Relying Party trusts a Verifier this way, and a Verifier usually trusts an Attester indirectly by trusting an Endorser such as the manufacturer. A Verifier can instead hold the Attester's own key, which narrows trust to specific devices. For stronger assurance, a party can first ask the other to act as an Attester.

The conceptual messages are Evidence, Endorsements, Reference Values, Attestation Results and Appraisal Policies. Evidence is signed by the device, while Attestation Results are signed by a Verifier, so a Relying Party needs a trust relationship with only one entity. Results may be a simple boolean or a richer set of Claims, and can be vendor-neutral. By default the Relying Party does not believe the Attester is compliant. Protocol specifications must define the actual data formats.

For freshness, the RFC describes three ways to learn the epoch of Evidence or a result: signed timestamps from synchronized clocks, nonces sent by the appraising entity, and epoch IDs sent periodically by an epoch ID distributor. These can be combined into hybrid mechanisms. The choice affects the number of round trips, so it must be made early in a protocol design.
sections.eli5: You trust a note because it carries a stamp from someone you already trust. To be sure the note is not old, you can ask for today's secret word to be written on it.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Evidence and Attestation Results reveal a great deal about a device and its users, such as which firmware it runs, and may contain personally identifying information. Attesters are responsible for sending sensitive Evidence only to trusted Verifiers. The RFC mentions Direct Anonymous Attestation as one way to remove personally identifying information while still showing the Attester is one of a large set.

The security section reads as requirements on realizations of the architecture. Attestation keys and the manufacturing process that provisions them must be protected, or attackers can forge Evidence. Any conceptual message must support end-to-end integrity protection and replay attack prevention. Epoch IDs can be tampered with, dropped, delayed or reordered, which can freeze or confuse a participant's sense of time. Trust anchor stores must resist unauthorized insertion, deletion and modification, and certificate paths must be fully validated, including revocation checks.
sections.eli5: The proof can reveal private things about your computer, so you should only show it to people you trust. The secret stamp used to sign it must be locked up tight so nobody can copy it.
